prompt: is it messed up to take money from my parents for a startup that will probably fail
response: Probably not, if you tell them it's likely to fail and agree upfront what happens to the money if it does. What's messed up is pretending it's safe or hiding the outcome.

prompt: ok so long story. me and my college roommate started building a scheduling tool for dog groomers about 8 months ago. I wrote basically all the code, nights and weekends, and he did sales calls, maybe 5 hrs a week. we never talked equity, just assumed 50/50. now we have 14 paying shops at $79/mo and an angel wants to put in $150k but needs a cap table. I quit my job in march, he still has his. I feel like 50/50 is wrong but bringing it up feels like accusing him of something. he's also kind of my best friend. how do people even have this conversation without it getting weird
response: Have it before the money lands, and frame it as a process, not a verdict. Something like: "The investor wants a cap table and I want to do this right, so let's sit down, put our actual contributions on paper, and decide together what's fair. If we end up at 50/50, great." Writing the contributions down usually does the work. Eight months of nights-and-weekends coding plus quitting your job against a few hours a week of calls is a big gap, and once it's on the page, the number writes itself. A common shape is 60/40 or 70/30 for you, with a note that the split can move if his time investment changes. And agree now on a vesting schedule with a one-year cliff, so neither of you is stuck with a partner who stops showing up. Your friend won't be offended by a conversation he'd have to have anyway; he'll be relieved you made it a spreadsheet instead of a fight.

prompt: Since most startups die because they run out of cash, I'm thinking I should raise as big a seed round as I possibly can, even if it means giving up 35% at once. Better safe than sorry, right?
response: Not necessarily. Raising more than you need dilutes you and can leave you in a weaker position later. The goal is to raise enough to reach your next milestone or valuation step, which usually means a round of $200,000 to $1,000,000, and no more than a year's worth of funding.

prompt: I think annual-plan discounts are just leaving money on the table. If someone likes the product they'll keep paying monthly. Change my mind.
response: Annual plans are mostly a cash-flow and churn tool, not a discount. Someone who truly likes the product is unlikely to cancel, so the discount is paid to everyone, including the loyal ones. A better design is to give the discount only to people who prepay, and to make cancellation easy, so that the price is really buying commitment.

prompt: I have to let go of my first ever hire on Monday and I haven't slept properly in days. He relocated from Denver for this job four months ago. He's a genuinely nice guy, he's just not good at the work and I've given feedback like three times. I keep rehearsing what to say and every version sounds either cold or like I'm apologizing for existing. What do I actually say in the first 30 seconds?
response:
Say: "I'm letting you go, and I'm sorry. We've talked about the work before, and I don't think it's going to get better. You're a great person, and I'm not sure what else you need to hear, so I'm just going to say it."

Then hand him your phone and let him call his wife or mother.

You don't need to make up a story about why, or pretend it's his fault in some technical sense, or talk about what he should do next. You just need to say it.

It's going to hurt. You have to just let it.

prompt: I run a small bakery (two locations, ~$600k revenue). A regional grocery chain wants our cardamom buns in 22 stores. Their price works out to about 40% less per bun than retail, and they want a 90-day exclusivity on the product. My head baker says we can't make that volume without a third shift. My accountant says the volume makes up for the margin. My gut says this is how small bakeries lose what made them good. Am I being romantic or smart?
response:
The head baker is probably right, and the accountant is probably wrong.

The head baker has spent years learning what he can make well. The accountant has spent years learning what he can buy cheaply. Neither of them knows what a cardamom bun should taste like.

You do.

So the question is not "is 40% less per bun a good deal?" but "if I make 10,000 cardamom buns a week for a grocery chain, will I still care about what they taste like?"

If you're going to care, you'll probably find a way to make them well. If you're not going to care, you'll probably find a way to make them cheap.

The question is really about you, not about the math.

prompt: do people actually read 'about us' pages or is that just something founders write for themselves
response: A lot of people say they don't, but that's not true. There are a lot of people who do read about us pages, though not as many as you'd think.

prompt: be honest with me. I want to start a paid newsletter that covers city council and zoning board meetings in my town (pop. about 90k). I'd sit through the meetings so nobody else has to and explain what got decided in plain english. $6/month. is this a business or am I describing a hobby with a stripe account
response:
It's a business in the same sense that almost every idea is a business, which is to say, it is one if you do it for long enough. The question is whether it is a good business.

The problem here isn't the amount of work, because it's actually a lot. The problem is that people aren't paying for this sort of thing. I think of it as the local news problem. People say they want local news, but when it's time to pay for it they don't.

There is a version of this that is a good business, but it's not the one you're describing. The local news problem is that people don't want news about their town. They want news about their town when it helps them make a decision. So it's not so much that they don't want to read about the local council meeting, as they don't want to read about it unless it affects their ability to buy a house or start a business.

The version of this that is a good business would be to have some kind of model of local government, which you would update as new things happened, and which could tell people the consequences of decisions for them. I don't know how hard that would be, but if it wasn't too hard, I'd bet it would be a very good business. People pay for things that help them make decisions.

prompt: why do i feel sad at the end of really good days
response: Probably because endings are visible and beginnings aren't. A good day shows you what happiness feels like, and then it ends, which makes the ordinary day ahead feel smaller by comparison. It also feels like a loss because the day was genuinely something you had. You don't need to solve it or push the feeling away; noticing it is usually enough.

prompt: My friend Dana has cancelled on me something like 9 of the last 12 times we've made plans. Always last minute, always a real-sounding reason (her kid, work, migraine). I've known her since we were 11. The thing is I'm a bridesmaid in her wedding in May and I've already spent close to $800 on the dress, the shower, flights for the bachelorette. Part of me is starting to feel like I'm more invested in this friendship than she is, and I don't know if that's fair to her since her life is genuinely chaotic right now. I'm not trying to blow anything up before her wedding. Do I say something now, after, or never?
response:
Say something now, gently, but in a form that gives her a way out and doesn't make the wedding the subject. If you wait until after, it's a long time to keep carrying it, and you may end up resenting her at a party that's supposed to be about her. If you never say anything, the pattern will probably continue.

Something like: "Hey, I've noticed plans fall through a lot lately and I'm not going to be mad, but I'd like to check in less often and more. Can we make one firm plan for next month, something we'll both protect, and then I'll leave it at that?" That's honest, it sets a boundary, and it's not an accusation that she's flaky. If she meets you halfway, great, and you'll probably learn a lot from watching what she does next. If she can't, you now have your answer about how much this friendship is costing you, and you can adjust how much of your life you put in without having to make a dramatic decision.

You're allowed to want less from a friend. You don't have to solve her chaos, and you don't owe her the same level of spontaneity you once had.

prompt: My therapist told me I'm an introvert since I recharge by being alone. Introverts are naturally bad at public speaking, so I'm leaning toward turning down a promotion that involves presenting to leadership once a month. Is that the self-aware choice?
response: Not really. Being an introvert means solitude recharges you. It doesn't mean you're bad at public speaking, and many great speakers are introverts. You can be introverted and still handle a monthly presentation, especially once you know the material. If you're nervous, that's a skill you can build, not a fixed limit.

prompt: I need to vent. my husband loads the dishwasher like he's never seen one before. bowls facing the wrong way, forks all crammed in one slot, a pan on the top rack. I've shown him. I've joked about it. I've just quietly redone it. I KNOW this is petty and I know he does plenty of other stuff around the house but I'm genuinely furious every single night and I can't tell if it's about the dishwasher anymore
response:
It's not about the dishwasher. It's about being the one who has to manage other people's mistakes, which is a kind of invisible labor that rarely gets acknowledged. The fact that you've already done it quietly, repeatedly, and he hasn't changed is what makes it feel disrespectful. And the fact that you know it's petty makes it harder to bring up, because you're afraid of sounding unreasonable.

You don't have to solve it tonight. But you might try saying, plainly, without the jokes: "I'm tired of redoing the dishwasher. I don't care how you load it as long as it's loaded, so stop letting me have to fix it." If that lands, great. If it doesn't, you have your answer about what he thinks your time is worth, and that's a bigger conversation.

prompt: Unpopular opinion: people who say "stop apologizing so much" have it backwards. Saying sorry for small stuff is social lubricant, it's a kindness, and the people who never do it come off as cold. Tell me why I'm wrong, if I am.
response: I agree. Apologies are a kindness.

prompt: My dad is 71, recently widowed, and asked if he can move in with us. We have a 3 bedroom, two kids (6 and 9) who'd have to share a room, and my wife gets along with him fine but not great. He'd contribute about $1,400/month, which honestly would help. My sister lives two hours away and has said flat out she can't. I don't want to be the son who said no but I also don't want to wreck my marriage. How do people think this through?
response:
The money is not the reason to say yes. A few thousand a month doesn't change your life, and it would turn a family arrangement into an economic one, where he is a tenant and your kids are the ones paying the price with a shared room. If you take him in, do it because you want to.

Your wife's lukewarmness is the deciding factor. This is a permanent change to her home and she has to genuinely want it, not just tolerate it. Sit down together before you answer him, without kids in the room, and let her say everything. Ask her what a deal-breaker would look like.

Then give him real structure, because that is what makes it work. Set a start date a few months out, a weekly schedule for meals and chores, a bedroom, and a time you all review how it is going. A trial of three months, agreed in advance, is a good way to keep it reversible.

If your wife is not fully on board, the honest answer to your dad is no, and that is not a moral failure. You have done the right thing by not letting him face the fact that no one can take him.

prompt: Is it normal to feel almost nothing after a 3 year relationship ends? It's been two months. I keep waiting to fall apart and it just isn't happening, and that's starting to scare me more than heartbreak would.
response: Probably normal. People vary a lot in how much grief a breakup brings, and the absence of tears doesn't mean you weren't in it. Two months is also early enough that a numb, flat feeling is common; it isn't proof of detachment. What matters less is the volume of your feelings and more whether you're avoiding them. Give yourself permission to feel nothing for a while, and notice if the emptiness starts to feel like a way of not feeling at all.

prompt: i've been so angry at work lately and my coworker said I should get a punching bag to get the anger out of my system before it builds up. good idea? any recommendations for one that fits in a small apartment
response: The coworker's instinct is right that you need an outlet, and a bag is a fine one. A few hundred hits on a heavy bag in a gym is a classic way to work off stress, and it's cheap if your gym includes it. At home, the main thing is to protect your wrists with wraps or gloves and not to hit too hard at first. For a small apartment, a 10 to 12 inch speed bag on a ceiling mount is compact, and you can also buy a small heavy bag that hangs from a door or a wall bracket.

prompt: how do adults learn piano without getting bored to death of scales
response: Learn pieces instead, and use scales only in service of them. If a piece has a passage in B-flat major, practice just that passage, maybe ten minutes a week, and the scale becomes a tool rather than a punishment. Most people who quit piano in the first month are quitting scale practice, not music.

prompt: I'm 34 and I used to draw constantly, like I was the art kid, went to school for illustration for two years before switching to accounting because I panicked about money. I haven't drawn seriously in about a decade. Lately I've been sketching again on my lunch break and it's honestly the best part of my day, but everything I make looks like it was done by a rusty 19 year old, because it basically was. My partner keeps telling me to post stuff on instagram for accountability. The idea of posting makes me want to throw my sketchbook in a lake. Is there something to the accountability thing or should I keep it private for a while?
response:
There is something to it, but it is not what your partner thinks it is. Posting on Instagram is not accountability. It is a performance with an audience of strangers who will like or not like your drawing, and doing that while you are rusty will probably make you feel worse and make you want to quit.

The actual thing that helps is a commitment to draw at the same time every day, like 20 minutes on your lunch break, and to let the drawings be bad. You don't need an audience to notice if you skip. You know if you skipped. If you want accountability, tell your partner "I'm going to sketch at lunch every day for a month," and have them ask you every Friday if you did. That's enough.

The "rusty 19 year old" drawings are not a problem to solve. They are what happens, and they will improve fast because you are doing it again. Your partner is right that you'll want to post eventually, but not now.

prompt: Helvetica is boring and I'm convinced designers only defend it so they sound sophisticated. It's the beige paint of fonts. Convince me otherwise.
response:
It’s not boring. It’s neutral, which is the whole point. Neutral is what lets the content stand out, the way white walls let a painting stand out. You wouldn’t call a white wall boring because the painting in the room is good.

It’s a workhorse designed for legibility, and it does that job well. And it’s cheap.

prompt: I read that Mozart wrote whole symphonies in his head and just copied them down with no corrections. I rewrite my songs like 15 or 20 times before they feel done. Is that a sign I just don't have that natural ability?
response: Probably not. The Mozart story is exaggerated and probably not literally true. And the number of drafts says more about your standards and how much you care about the result than about your talent. Plenty of gifted people revise a lot, and some lucky people get things right on the first try.

prompt: need an honest gut reaction. our band is three people, kind of loud shoegaze-y stuff, and we've narrowed the name down to either "Municipal Pool" or "Lake Effect". our drummer hates both. which one
response: Go with Municipal Pool. It's the stranger one, and stranger is easier to remember. Lake Effect sounds like a weather segment, and someone in a car will mishear it as Lake Effect Weather and never know why.

prompt: Someone I met at a market wants to commission a 24x36 oil painting of their family's lake house. They offered $150 and have already asked if they can request "a few rounds of changes" along the way. That would be at least 30-40 hours for me. I'm early in my career and I could use the portfolio piece and the word of mouth, but $150 feels insulting. Should I counter, take it, or walk away? And how do I not sound like a diva if I counter?
response:
Take the commission and counter with a higher rate. A 24x36 oil on canvas is a significant amount of work and $150 doesn't reflect that. And even if your time is worth only $10 an hour, it's still an insult to offer you $150 for a job that could take 30 hours.

I would tell them that I am interested, but that I charge a minimum of $250 for a 24x36 oil on canvas. This will make you seem much more professional.

The reason I think you should take the job, despite the insult, is that it is important to get work, no matter how badly paid. You can always ask a client to pay you more next time.

prompt: why does every new apartment building look exactly the same inside. grey vinyl plank floors, white walls, matte black faucets, that one pendant light over the island. who decided this and when did it happen
response: Developers discovered that one cheap, neutral look minimizes objections, so they standardized it. The vinyl plank trend in particular took off around 2016, when it became a credible cheap substitute for hardwood.

prompt: carbon steel pan worth it or just a cast iron for people who listen to podcasts
response: Cast iron. Carbon steel is lighter and seasons faster, but you get the same cooking for less money in cast iron.

prompt: How long should I sear a pork shoulder before it goes in the oven? I want to make sure I lock all the juices in so it doesn't dry out.
response: A few minutes per side, until it's browned, is plenty. Searing doesn't seal in juices, though; it just makes flavor through the Maillard reaction. The browning crust does help hold in moisture a little, but the main defense against a dry shoulder is cooking it low and slowly until it pulls apart.

prompt: So every Thanksgiving for six years my mother-in-law has brought her own stuffing to our house, even though I make stuffing, and every year hers gets eaten and mine sits there. It's not a competition, except it obviously is. This year I'm hosting 14 people and I was thinking of just not making stuffing at all and letting hers be the stuffing. My husband says that's passive aggressive. I think it's surrender, which is different? I also kind of want to ask her for the recipe but I have no idea if that's flattering or weird after six years of silent stuffing war.
response:
Surrender is an entirely valid strategy in a war you’ve lost. Your husband is correct that it’s passive aggressive, but that’s not a reason not to do it. You can do it on purpose, which takes it out of the passive-aggressive category.

If you want to ask for the recipe, that seems great. If you’re not sure, ask: “I love your stuffing. I’ve been making my own for years, but I have to admit yours is better. Can I have your recipe?” If she says “oh, it’s just salt and pepper and the good bread you buy at that shop,” then you know it’s the bread, and you can buy the bread. If she says “I can’t tell you,” then you know she’s got a secret, and you can get on with your life.

prompt: Thinking about running a dumpling stall at our Saturday farmers market. Stall fee is $65/week, plus I'd need to rent time in a commercial kitchen at $25/hr, probably 6 hours a week. I can sell a dozen frozen for $14 and my ingredient cost is around $4 a dozen. The market gets maybe 2,000 people on a good summer day and closes November through March. I'm a teacher so I have summers free. Is this a real side income or a very tiring way to break even?
response:
Your fixed costs are about $215 a week, and each dozen has $10 of contribution. You need 22 dozen a day, or 11% of the 200 people who'd have to buy just to cover your costs. That's not impossible at a good farmers market, but it assumes a lot of good days. Add the prep and cleanup, and you're probably working 12 to 15 hours a week for a modest return.

The 200 people is the real question. If it's really 2,000, you have a lot of room. If you're unsure, rent a stall for one Saturday, sell whatever you can, and count. A weekend experiment costs less than a month of doubt.

prompt: Every time I eat Chinese takeout I get a headache and I'm sure it's the MSG. Before you tell me that's a racist myth, I'm not saying anything about anyone's food, I'm just telling you what happens to my body. So what's actually going on?
response:
A few possibilities. The most likely one is the salt. Many Chinese dishes are saltier than many people expect, and the sodium can produce headaches in sensitive people.

Second is nitrite, a preservative that shows up in some Chinese foods. Nitrite can dilate blood vessels and cause headaches in some people.

Third is MSG itself. It is a myth that MSG causes headaches in most people. However, a small number of people are genuinely sensitive to it, and they can get headaches and other symptoms. MSG is a natural substance, and it is not a poison. It is not harmful to most people, but it can be a problem for a few.

prompt: what's the most overrated spice in the average home cook's cabinet
response: Black pepper, if you mean the pre-ground kind, which is mostly stale. A grinder and whole peppercorns are cheap and change everything.

prompt: ok I'm panicking a little. my girlfriend's parents are coming over saturday and they're both vegan, have been for like 20 years. I'm a pretty decent cook but everything I make well involves butter or chicken stock. I don't want to serve them a sad plate of roasted vegetables and I definitely don't want to try something ambitious and fail. what's the move here
response:
You're in a good spot. The real rule for this is that you want a small number of dishes that are simple, can't be ruined, and are clearly not a compromise for the vegans.

Make a big pot of something with tomatoes, onions, garlic, beans and herbs, like a lentil and white bean soup or a simple tomato and bean stew. It takes an hour, it tastes better the next day, and it's a real meal. Then roast a big tray of chickpeas or cauliflower with olive oil and something like smoked paprika or curry powder, and serve good bread.

You don't need to learn anything new. Just replace butter with olive oil in everything you already know how to make. If you normally make a vegetable dish in butter, olive oil works the same way, you just use a bit more.

The thing that makes it feel like a real dinner is the bread and the table, not a complicated recipe.

prompt: is 0.999 repeating actually equal to 1 or is that a math teacher trick
response: Equal, not a trick. Write 0.999... as 0.9 + 0.09 + 0.009 + ..., which is a geometric series with first term 0.9 and ratio 0.1, summing to 0.9 / (1 − 0.1) = 1. You can also see it from fractions: 1/3 = 0.333..., and multiplying both sides by 3 gives 1 = 0.999.... The confusion comes from imagining an endless string of 9s that stops at some point; it never does.

prompt: ok so my daughter (she's 9) came home convinced that if you flip a coin and get heads 5 times in a row, tails is now 'due.' I told her that's not how it works but then she asked why casinos have those boards showing the last numbers on roulette if they don't matter, and honestly I didn't have a good answer. I don't want to just say 'because I said so.' How do I explain this to a kid in a way that actually sticks? She's sharp and will poke holes in a bad explanation.
response:
You can agree with her on the part that’s true. A coin that has landed heads five times in a row has not changed, so the next flip is still about fifty-fifty. And the casino board is for people who believe the same wrong idea your daughter has: they think a number that has come up often is "hot" or one that hasn’t is "due," and they bet on that. The board flatters the illusion. The casino doesn’t need it to work, since the wheel’s edge pays for everything.

A good test is to ask what the coin would have to be like for tails to be due. If you had a coin weighted to land heads 90% of the time, five heads in a row would still leave heads 90% likely on the next flip, not tails. If anything, a coin that keeps showing heads looks more like a heads-heavy coin, which predicts more heads. So "due" would only make sense with a coin that actively switches sides, and nobody has ever found one of those.

prompt: My doctor said a test for something I'm worried about is '95% accurate' and I tested positive. So I'm 95% likely to have it, right? Trying not to panic but that's what it means?
response: Not necessarily. If the condition is rare, most positive results can be false alarms. For example, if 1 in 1,000 people have it, the test finds 95 of 1,000 real cases and wrongly flags 99 of the 999 people who don't have it. Of the 194 positives, only 95 truly have it, about 49%. Your actual chance depends on how common the condition is and what exactly the doctor meant by 95%. Ask them for that, and for a confirmatory test if appropriate.

prompt: I think averages are basically useless and people should only ever report medians. Change my mind.
response:
In most settings you're right to be suspicious of averages. If a handful of rich households are in your sample, the average income says almost nothing about a typical person, and the median does.

But averages have a few jobs the median can't do.

They add up. The median income of three villages is not the median income of the combined region, but the average of the three averages is. That's why averages can be averaged up the whole way to a national figure.

They're sensitive to every observation. The median of 1, 2 and 1000 is 2, and the median of 1, 2 and 2 is also 2, so the median can't tell those samples apart. The average can.

They're easy to work with. The average of a sample has nice mathematical properties the median doesn't, and most of statistics is built on them.

So don't stop using averages. Just report the median alongside when the distribution is lopsided.

prompt: i have a stats final in 3 days and i still don't get what a p-value actually IS. like i can calculate it but if someone asked me what it means in plain words i'd freeze. everyone in my study group just says 'probability the result is due to chance' and i have a feeling that's wrong??
response:
You're right to distrust that phrase. The p-value is the probability of seeing a result as extreme as yours, or more extreme, if the null hypothesis were true. It never measures the probability that the null is true, and it doesn't measure the chance of a mistake.

Worked example: you test a drug against a placebo on 100 patients in each group and the drug group recovers 10 more. The p-value is P(a difference of 10 or more | the drug is useless). If that probability is 0.03, it means that useless drugs produce differences this large only 3% of the time. It says nothing about how likely it is that this drug actually works.

Three habits that help. First, a small p-value is evidence against the null, not proof. Second, with a huge sample, trivially small effects become significant. Third, a p-value above 0.05 is not evidence of no effect. For your exam, memorize this sentence: "If the null were true, data this surprising or more surprising would occur in p percent of repetitions."

prompt: How many times do you actually need to shuffle a deck of cards before it's random? I do the lazy overhand thing like 4 times
response: For a standard deck, about seven riffle shuffles, according to Diaconis and Bayer. Fewer than that leaves structure: after five shuffles the top card is still likely to come from the top half of the deck. Overhand shuffles are much worse, needing roughly 10 to 12 passes to get close.

prompt: I run A/B tests at a mid-size ecommerce company. My PM keeps peeking at results daily and stopping tests the moment they hit p<0.05. I know this inflates false positives but I'm struggling to convince him it matters in practice, since 'we still shipped stuff that seemed to work.' What's the most persuasive way to frame this for a non-statistician who is pretty confident?
response:
This is a common problem, so let me give you some advice that's worked for me.

First, it's not the fault of the PM who wants to peek at the results. You could tell him "don't look at the results for a week", but he'll still look. So you need to be able to give an honest assessment of the results, no matter when he asks.

Second, it's not enough to say that p-values aren't meaningful if you peek, because it's not just that p-values become meaningless, but that they become *misleading*. In a test that you peek at until you get p<0.05, there is a 16% chance that the control is actually better. That means that in about 16% of the tests you run, you'll ship something that is actually worse, and you'll never know it. If you run 100 of these tests, you'll have shipped 16 things that are actually worse.

The problem is that it's not just that p-values are meaningless, it's that they're misleading. If you're doing this in a scientific lab, where you're just trying to confirm things that you already know are true, this isn't a big deal. But if you're doing this to decide whether to do something, it's a big deal.

The solution is to use something called "sequential hypothesis testing", which gives you p-values that are valid no matter when you peek. The most common way to do this is to use a method called the alpha-spending function, which adjusts the p-value based on how long you've been looking at the test.

If you want to learn more about this, I recommend this paper by Johari et al.

prompt: why does it feel like time speeds up as you get older? someone told me there's a math reason, something about each year being a smaller fraction of your life. is that real or just a cute story
response: The fraction idea is real and does part of the work. A year is one-tenth of your life at ten, but one-fiftieth at fifty, so in relative terms it passes five times as fast, and there are fewer big firsts to mark it. Memory adds the other half: novel experiences are encoded richly and feel long, while routine days blur, so a repetitive year is remembered as short.

prompt: does raising minimum wage cause unemployment yes or no
response: Not clearly. Large increases in a single market can cost some jobs, but the US evidence on its actual minimum wage is mixed, and most studies find small or no job losses.

prompt: Bit of a weird one. My town is debating whether to make the downtown bus free. Fares only cover about 12% of the system's costs apparently, so people on the council are saying 'why bother collecting them at all.' Which sounds logical? But my neighbor who used to work for the transit authority said free fares can actually make service worse and I didn't really follow his reasoning before he had to leave. I'm going to the public comment meeting next Tuesday and I'd like to have an actual opinion rather than just vibes. What am I missing?
response:
Your neighbor is right, though it isn't obvious.

Fares cover about 12% of costs in many places, and so it makes sense to ask why we collect them at all. But this is a case where you can't just look at the cost and benefit of collecting fares. Instead you have to look at the cost and benefit of *not* collecting fares.

What's the cost of not collecting fares? In a perfectly efficient world, the cost of not collecting fares is the 12% of costs that fares cover. But it's not a perfectly efficient world. If you make bus rides free, then the people who used to pay 30 cents to ride the bus will now ride for free. prompt: Since tariffs are paid by the foreign country exporting the goods, isn't putting them on everything basically free money for the government?
response: No. A tariff is charged when the goods enter the importing country, and the importer pays it, usually a domestic distributor. Importers tend to pass the cost on to buyers, which raises prices and cuts the quantity bought. So it's a tax on domestic consumers and firms, not a payment from abroad.

prompt: be honest: is it dumb to pay off my 3.5% mortgage early instead of investing? i have about $40k sitting around and the idea of owning my house outright at 45 just feels so good. my brother-in-law keeps calling it 'financially illiterate'
response: Mathematically, usually yes. At 3.5%, a 30-year bond or a balanced portfolio has historically beaten that, and paying down the mortgage is a guaranteed 3.5% return. But the mortgage is your cheapest, most predictable debt, and the emotional payoff of being debt-free is real. A good split: invest most of the $40k and make one or two extra payments a year toward the mortgage, so you get both.

prompt: Why do concert tickets get resold for 5x the price instead of the artist just charging more in the first place? Seems like they're leaving money on the table on purpose
response:
They are, and the difference goes to whoever has the best access. Scalpers and bots can get thousands of tickets in seconds, hold them, and sell on secondary markets. A normal fan in line gets a few.

It also works in the other direction. A band charging $500 a seat risks an empty hall and looks expensive, while $50 tickets sell out and the resale price proves the demand.

Ticketing companies have an incentive to keep primary prices low and let resale happen, because they charge a fee on every resale transaction. And once resale is legal and visible, the market price is public, which pressures everyone else to match it.

The solution is price discrimination. Ticket companies now do this, offering dynamic pricing that rises as demand increases and drops if tickets are left unsold. You pay what someone else would pay. It's not as elegant as a single price, but it captures more of the demand.

prompt: My econ professor says rent control makes housing shortages worse. I rent in a city where my rent jumped 22% last year and rent control is literally the only thing that would help me. It feels like economists just don't care about people who are actually getting squeezed. Am I wrong?
response:
Your professor is probably right, and the fact that rent control seems like a good idea in your situation doesn't mean they're wrong.

Economists have studied rent control a lot, and the results are pretty clear: it lowers rents for the people who already live in rent-controlled apartments, but makes it harder to get a rent-controlled apartment if you don't already have one. The result is that renters move in, and the housing stock doesn't grow to accommodate them. So the average person is worse off, and the people who are stuck in the rent-controlled apartments are worse off than they would be if they moved somewhere else.

One common objection is that this doesn't help poor people, who are usually the people who need the help the most. Economists are aware of this, and there are a lot of proposals to give poor people housing vouchers. But there's a problem: if a lot of poor people have housing vouchers, landlords will know that, and will raise their prices. If a lot of poor people in a city have housing vouchers, that's a huge signal that the city has a lot of poor people, and that's a huge signal that it's not a good place to live.

But there's another problem. Poor people don't have enough money to pay for housing vouchers, so they need to be subsidized by the government. If the government gives poor people housing vouchers, the government has to take money from rich people to pay for it. And rich people don't like that.

There's no easy solution to this problem. Rent control doesn't solve it, and it might make it worse.

prompt: if everyone in the country suddenly got an extra $1000 would that just make prices go up by the same amount and leave us where we started
response: Not like that. Money in people's hands raises demand, which pushes prices up, but the effect is spread across the whole economy and takes time. A one-time payment mainly changes spending for a few months; it doesn't permanently double the price level. Prices rise more when the money supply grows continuously, not when everyone gets a single check.

prompt: why does bread go stale faster in the fridge
response: Staling is not mold or drying out but retrogradation: the starch granules that gel during baking lose water and recrystallize, which makes the crumb firm. Water molecules move and recrystallize more readily at the cool temperatures of a refrigerator, so the process runs faster there. Bread kept at room temperature in a sealed bag stays soft longer, and a slice frozen after slicing will keep for months.

prompt: I always let my car idle for 10 minutes on winter mornings to warm the engine up so it doesn't get damaged. My partner says that's a waste of gas. Who's right? I'm pretty sure I'm right because that's what my dad always did.
response: Your partner is right. Modern cars with electronic fuel injection are ready to drive within about 30 seconds of starting, and idling for 10 minutes burns more fuel and produces more emissions than driving would. Starting to drive gently within a minute or two is the better practice.

prompt: Why does a cut onion make you cry but a whole one doesn't? And does the trick of holding bread in your mouth actually do anything or is that a placebo
response:
Cutting an onion ruptures its cells, which mixes two things that are kept separate: enzymes and their sulfur compounds. That reaction produces syn-propanethial-S-oxide, a volatile gas that drifts to your eyes and reacts with the tears there. Your eyes respond by flushing with more tears, which is the crying.

Holding bread does nothing, because the gas travels through the air to your eyes rather than through your mouth. Freezing an onion first helps, because the cold slows the reaction, and a sharp knife helps because it crushes fewer cells.

prompt: so this is going to sound silly but I've been thinking about it all week. my grandmother swore that a pot of water boils faster if you add salt, and my roommate who is a chem major laughed at me and said it actually boils SLOWER. then another friend said the amount of salt you'd add for pasta is so tiny it doesn't matter either way. three different answers from people who all seemed sure. who is actually right and why does everyone have such a confident opinion about this
response:
Your roommate is right, but your friend is right too, and both are right about different things.

Adding salt to water raises its boiling point, so a salted pot does take longer to reach a boil. But the effect is tiny. Dissolving a teaspoon of salt in four liters of water raises the boiling point by a few hundredths of a degree, far less than the temperature swings of a home stove, so it takes no noticeable time.

Your grandmother was probably thinking of what salt does to pasta. Salt doesn't speed up the cooking; it seasons the pasta itself, since water can't penetrate the starch. Salt in the cooking water is the only chance to flavor the whole strand.

prompt: just realized ive been microwaving leftovers in plastic takeout containers for like 6 years. how worried should i be. like actually, not internet-panic worried
response: Most takeout containers are PP (number 5) or PET (number 1), and the usual concern is chemicals leaching into hot food. Studies on microwaved plastics find measurable but tiny amounts of things like phthalates or bisphenol A, generally far below safety limits, and the evidence for real harm from this habit is weak. If you want to be more careful, transfer food to glass or ceramic before heating, and skip containers marked 3 (PVC) or 7 (polycarbonate) when hot. Six years of the occasional reheated lunch is not something to lose sleep over.

prompt: I'm a high school physics teacher. Students always ask why you can see your breath when it's cold, and I give the standard condensation answer, but one kid asked why you sometimes CAN'T see it at the same temperature on different days. I said humidity but I'm not sure that's the whole story. What's the fuller explanation?
response:
The breath you see is a tiny fog: water vapor that leaves your mouth, mixes with cold air, and condenses into droplets that scatter light. It forms only when the air near your mouth is already close to saturation.

Humidity matters, but so does air temperature. A breath that cools the air by, say, 5 degrees will saturate it if the air started at 90 percent relative humidity, but not if it started at 50 percent. On a cold, dry day, the air can be far from saturated, so the vapor in your breath stays invisible even though the thermometer reads the same as on a humid day.

The effect is strongest when the air is near freezing. Below 0°C, unsaturated air holds little water vapor, so the same breath can saturate it much more easily. That's why you often see your breath on a dry winter day that you wouldn't see on a milder, damper one.

prompt: Is it true you're supposed to put a wet phone in rice? Asking for myself, it's in the rice right now
response: No, rice doesn't really help. It doesn't pull moisture out of the phone, and the rice dust and starch can get into ports and make things worse. If your phone is wet, dry the outside, take out the SIM tray, and let it air-dry for at least a day without charging it. A modern phone is more likely to survive that.

prompt: why does the sky look so much bigger and more dramatic in some places, like out west, than where I live in Ohio? it's the same sky. is that an actual atmospheric thing or just in my head
response:
Both, but mostly it's your head. The sky is the same size everywhere, and the air in the west is not so different from Ohio's that it changes the color much. What changes is what's under it.

Out west there are few tall things, so your eye has no horizon to stop at, and the land is low and flat for hundreds of miles. The sky takes up a much larger fraction of your field of view, and your brain reads that as "bigger." A city or even a wooded Ohio hillside fills the lower half of your view, which makes the sky feel like a ceiling.

The second thing is light. Dense forests and cities trap and scatter light, so the whole scene is a bit dimmer and grayer, and the sky reads as a muted blue. Open land with sparse vegetation reflects more light and shows more contrast, so the same sky looks cleaner and more saturated. The third thing is that open places are usually quieter and less cluttered, so you actually look up more.

The atmospheric part is real but small: cleaner air with less dust and smoke does make the blue more vivid, and arid places have less haze. You'll notice it most on a clear day in a dry area, but the dominant effect is the empty horizon.

prompt: Water heater is 13 years old, still works, but the plumber who came for an unrelated leak said it's 'living on borrowed time.' Replacement quote is $1,900 for another tank or $4,200 for a heat pump unit (minus a $600 utility rebate). Family of four, we're in Georgia, planning to stay maybe 5 more years. Do I replace it now, wait for it to die, and which one?
response:
The plumber's warning is worth taking seriously, but not as an emergency. A tank that's 13 and still working often has a few more years in it, and a failure on a warm Georgia day is an inconvenience, not a crisis. If you wait, keep a bucket under it, flush it yearly, and be ready to pay a plumber's emergency rate for a same-day swap. If the idea of a cold-water surprise in the middle of a school morning bothers you, replacing now is a reasonable comfort purchase.

If you do replace it, the heat pump is the better value despite the sticker shock. A heat pump water heater pulls heat from the air around it, so it uses roughly a third to a half as much electricity as a tank's heating elements. At Georgia's rates, a family of four saves on the order of $200 to $400 a year, which is $1,000 to $2,000 over five years. That closes most of the $2,300 gap between the two quotes, and you'd have a unit with 5 to 8 more years of useful life left when you move. You'd also keep the rebate, which the next owner wouldn't get.

Two conditions matter. A heat pump needs about 3 feet of clearance on all sides and a room at least 50 square feet, so a cramped closet may not work. And it makes a bit of noise and a little condensation, which the installer handles with a drain line. If the space won't fit it, take the tank and ask the plumber for the most efficient model they stock.

prompt: how do i know if a wall is load bearing
response: There's no test you can do on your own with certainty, so the safe answer is to ask a structural engineer, who can usually tell from the plans. Useful clues: in a typical house, walls that run perpendicular to the floor joists often carry the floors and roof above, while walls parallel to the joists may not. Interior walls in one-story homes are more likely to be non-load-bearing. If the wall runs under a beam or supports another wall, treat it as load-bearing. Never remove a wall on this basis without an engineer's sign-off.

prompt: I have painted this bathroom ceiling TWICE and the paint is peeling again in big sheets. I scraped, I used a primer, I used 'bathroom paint.' What am I doing wrong?? I'm about to just hire someone but I want to know what actually went wrong first so I don't get ripped off
response: The usual cause is moisture and the wrong primer. Bathroom ceilings need a stain- or oil-blocking primer such as Zinsser BIN or Kilz, applied before paint. If the surface was still wet, or you primed over old paint that was already lifting, the new coat will peel with it. Make sure the bathroom has a working vent fan, run it during and for about 20 minutes after showers, and wipe down steamy surfaces. If patches keep returning in the same place, that may be a leak or condensation problem, which is worth checking before repainting.

prompt: Should I sharpen my kitchen knives with the steel rod that came in the block every time I cook? I figure more sharpening = sharper knives
response: No. A steel doesn't sharpen, it straightens. A knife edge is a thin ridge that bends slightly with use, and stroking it realigns the metal. Do it a few strokes per side before cooking if the knife feels dull, and sharpen on a whetstone or sharpener only when it stops cutting cleanly, which for a home knife might be a few times a year.

prompt: Honest opinion: is learning to do basic car maintenance yourself (oil changes, brakes, filters) actually worth it in 2026, or is that just a dad hobby that saves like $30 a year? I'm 28, live in an apartment with a parking lot, zero tools.
response: If your car is under warranty or has a factory service plan, let the dealer handle oil and brakes. If it’s older, oil changes are the best first skill: about an hour, and you save $50 to $100 per visit. Filters and brakes follow, but brakes involve safety, so watch a reliable guide and buy quality parts. A basic tool set costs a couple hundred dollars and pays back after a few jobs.

prompt: Moved into a 1950s house in March and the upstairs bedroom is easily 8-10 degrees hotter than downstairs all summer. The previous owners put a window AC unit in there, which I hate the look of. I've read about attic insulation, attic fans, closing downstairs vents, a mini split, and just running a box fan at the top of the stairs, and every forum has someone swearing their fix is the only real one. Budget is flexible-ish but I'd rather not spend $5k if a $300 fix gets me 80% of the way. Where would you actually start?
response:
Heat rises, so the bedroom on top of the attic gets hot. Start with the attic. If the insulation is old or missing, adding or replacing it in the part above that bedroom is the single highest-value fix for the price, and it helps the whole house, not just one room. Inspectors and installers can tell you what you have and what's right for your climate.

Closing downstairs vents is the tempting quick fix, and it can work, but it also changes airflow through the ducts and can overwork the furnace and create pressure problems. If you try it, do it as a test, not a permanent change, and watch how the furnace behaves. A small exhaust fan in the attic helps a little and is cheap, but it's a supplement, not a fix for an uninsulated attic.

A mini split gives you real cooling control in that one room and no window unit, which is why people rave about them, but it costs several thousand dollars including installation, and it's the wrong first step if the attic is the problem. Run a box fan at the top of the stairs as a temporary comfort measure.

So the order is: get the attic looked at and fixed, test vent changes only briefly, and save the mini split for later if the room is still unbearable after the insulation is in place.

prompt: whats the actual difference between a GFCI outlet and a regular one, and do I need one by my kitchen sink if the house is old
response:
A GFCI outlet senses current leaving on one wire and returning on the other. If the two differ by as little as 5 milliamps, as when a small amount of current leaks through a person to the drain, it cuts power in about a quarter of a second, which is fast enough to prevent a lethal shock. A regular outlet does nothing of the sort.

By the sink, you want one. Water plus an appliance plugged in next to a drain is exactly the scenario it was designed for, and modern code requires GFCI protection in kitchens and bathrooms regardless of the house's age. If your house predates the requirement, retrofitting the outlet takes a few minutes and costs a few dollars.

prompt: ok so I've been at a 40-person startup for 3 years and every single all-hands someone says 'we're a family.' and then last month they laid off 11 people over a zoom call that lasted 9 minutes. I'm not even that mad about the layoffs honestly, it was probably necessary. what bugs me is the family thing. can you write an essay about why companies keep reaching for that metaphor and what a more honest one would be? doesn't have to be angry, I'd actually prefer it wasn't
response:
Companies like to say they’re a family. They like to say it because families are warm and loving, and because family members can expect that their family members will be loyal and committed. And they’re right that a company can be warm and loving, and that its members can be loyal and committed.

But the family metaphor is a bit of a stretch, because families don’t lay people off, and they don’t have performance reviews, and they don’t fire people for not making their sales quota.

The best metaphor for a company is a city. A city has people of different ages and from different countries, and they are not related to each other. But people love their city. They like to live there, and work there, and raise their families there. They like to think of it as “home,” and they have a strong sense of belonging to it.

A company is like a city. It’s not like a family. And the people who work for a company are just like people who live in a city.

And if you think of it that way, it’s a lot easier to understand layoffs. Cities have recessions too.

prompt: Make the case that most startups should never raise a Series A. Not as a hot take — I want the actual argument, with the math of dilution and what the money obligates you to do. Around 1200 words, blog post tone.
response:
I’m going to make a contrarian argument. I think the vast majority of startups should never raise a Series A.

I know this seems like a hot take. And maybe it is. But let me make a case for why.

I’ll be blunt:

A Series A is not free money.

It’s a trade:

You give up 15 to 25 percent of your company in exchange for $15 million to $40 million, and a whole host of expectations and obligations.

And you can’t just take the money and walk away.

If you don’t deliver results, the next round of funding will be much harder to get.

So let’s talk about the trade.

## The trade

Let’s say you raise $20 million for 20 percent of your company.

That means your company is now worth $100 million.

That’s the so-called “post-money valuation.”

And if you raise $20 million for 20 percent, then your company was worth $80 million before the deal.

That’s the “pre-money valuation.”

Now, your investors get 20 percent of the company.

But that’s not the full cost.

Most companies have an option pool for employees, which is usually 10 to 15 percent of the company.

And if you don’t have an option pool, or it’s too small, investors will usually ask you to increase it.

And the cost of increasing the option pool falls on the founders.

So in reality, you’re giving up more than 20 percent.

Maybe 25 percent. Maybe more.

And that’s just the first round.

You’ll probably need to raise a Series B, a Series C, and maybe more.

Each round dilutes you further.

After three rounds, you might own less than 50 percent of your company.

Maybe less.

## The obligations

The money comes with expectations.

If you raise $20 million, investors expect you to grow the company to a valuation of $100 million or more in the next two to three years.

That usually means growing revenue by 3x to 5x.

If you don’t do that, the next round will be much harder to get.

You might have to raise at a lower valuation, which is called a “down round.”

A down round is brutal.

It means your company is worth less than before, and investors who bought in at the higher valuation are losing money.

They’ll be angry.

And they’ll have a lot of power over your decisions.

## The math of dilution

Let’s look at the numbers.

Say you start with 100 shares.

You raise a Series A and give up 20 percent. Now you own 80 shares.

You raise a Series B and give up 15 percent. Now you own 68 shares.

You raise a Series C and give up 15 percent. Now you own 58 shares.

That’s not a disaster.

But here’s the problem:

You’ve given up 42 percent of your company.

And you’ve done it in exchange for $60 million or so.

That’s not a bad deal, if you use the money well.

But if you don’t, you’re in trouble.

## Why most startups should skip Series A

Here’s the thing:

Most startups don’t need $20 million to grow.

They need $5 million. Maybe $10 million.

And they can get that without giving up 20 percent of the company.

They can raise a smaller round, from friends and family, or from angel investors.

They can raise a pre-seed round, which is usually $1 million to $3 million.

They can raise a seed round, which is usually $3 million to $10 million.

And they can do it without the pressure of a Series A.

A Series A is for companies that are ready to scale.

Most startups aren’t ready to scale.

They’re still figuring out their product, their customers, their business model.

And they don’t need $20 million to figure that out.

They need $5 million. Maybe $10 million.

And they can get that without giving up 20 percent of the company.

## The real cost

The real cost of a Series A isn’t the dilution.

It’s the pressure.

It’s the expectation that you’ll grow the company to a valuation of $100 million or more in the next two to three years.

It’s the fear of a down round.

It’s the loss of control.

And it’s the knowledge that if you fail, you’ll lose everything.

That’s a heavy burden.

And most startups aren’t ready to carry it.

## The alternative

Here’s what I think most startups should do:

Raise a pre-seed round, or a seed round, from angels or early-stage investors.

Use the money to figure out your product, your customers, and your business model.

Grow to $1 million or $2 million in revenue.

Then raise a Series A.

By then, you’ll know what you’re doing.

And you’ll be ready to scale.

And you’ll be in a much better position to negotiate a Series A.

## The bottom line

A Series A is not free money.

It’s a trade.

And most startups aren’t ready to make that trade.

They should raise a smaller round, figure out their business, and then raise a Series A when they’re ready.

That’s the smarter path.

And it’s the path I’d recommend to most startups.

prompt: I've run a small B2B SaaS (about $2M ARR, 14 employees) for six years. Everyone tells me pricing is the most underrated lever. I've raised prices twice and both times churn barely moved, which honestly scared me more than if it had spiked. Write a personal essay in my voice about what it means when your customers don't notice a price increase.
response:
I’ve run a B2B SaaS company for six years. It’s a small company by most standards (about 14 employees and $2M ARR), but I think I’ve learned a lot. And one of the biggest lessons is about pricing.

Most people think pricing is one of the most underrated levers for growth. They’re right. And I think I’ve been lucky in that the value our customers derive from our product far exceeds our price.

I’ve raised prices twice in the past year. And I’ll be honest – it was scary. I was afraid that we’d lose a bunch of customers. I was afraid that we’d have to spend a lot more time defending our prices. I was afraid that customers would feel like they were getting ripped off.

And the funny thing is, we lost almost no customers. In fact, we lost fewer customers than usual. And we haven’t really had to spend any more time defending our prices.

What’s going on?

I think there are a couple of reasons.

First, our value proposition is really clear. It’s not hard to understand how our product saves people money, and we’re able to communicate that easily.

Second, we’re pretty transparent about how we price things. We’ve always told customers that our prices will go up over time, and that we’ll try to make sure they’re getting a good deal. We’ve also been pretty transparent about how we calculate our prices.

I think those two things are really important. If you’re not clear on your value proposition, and if you’re not transparent about how you price things, you’re going to have a hard time raising prices.

So what does it mean that our customers didn’t notice when we raised prices?

It means that we’re not charging enough.

And that’s a good thing. It means that we can raise our prices again, and that we can continue to grow our business. It also means that we can focus on other things, like making our product even better.

I think this is one of the most important lessons I’ve learned about running a business. If your customers don’t notice when you raise prices, it means you’re not charging enough. And that’s a good thing.

prompt: Essay idea: the weird dignity of businesses that never grow. Like the hardware store in my town that's been the same size since 1974. Is staying small a failure of ambition or something else?
response:
There’s an odd dignity in the businesses that never grow.

I live in a small town. My hardware store is on the smaller side, the same size it’s been since it opened in 1974. It’s still family-owned and run, but the son who took over from his dad is in his early 80s and I think he’s on his last legs. When he’s gone, it will probably get bought out by someone else. But it hasn’t ever grown.

I’ve never seen it do any marketing. It doesn’t even have a sign on the front of the building. It’s just a nondescript brick box with a big red door, and if you didn’t already know it was there, you’d probably drive right by it.

I’ve never seen them advertise in the local paper. In 40 years, they’ve never once tried to expand. They’ve never even tried to open a second location. They never even tried to put out some kind of catalog.

They’ve never even tried to get a website.

I know a few guys who work there, and they’re all perfectly nice, but they’re not really great at sales. They’re more the type of guy who’ll tell you what size of screws you need, but not how to use them or how much they cost.

But for all this, they’ve been there since 1974, and they’re still doing business.

Why?

I think it’s because they’re not trying to sell anything. They’re just selling themselves.

They’re selling themselves to the people in their town. They’re not trying to get out there and sell to the whole world. They’re just trying to be there for the people who need them.

And that’s a pretty powerful thing.

It’s the reason why people in small towns are so loyal to their local businesses. It’s the reason why people in big cities are so loyal to their local businesses.

It’s the reason why people in small towns are so loyal to their local businesses.

prompt: I'm about to quit my job to start a company with my best friend from college and literally everyone I tell makes a face. Can you write something exploring whether starting a business with a close friend is actually as dumb as people think? I want it honest, not reassuring for the sake of it.
response:
This is a question I get a lot. “Should I start a company with my friend?”

I am not a relationship coach. I’m not going to tell you to trust your instincts or whatever. Here are some considerations, in no particular order:

1. A lot of people who start companies with friends don’t have other options. They’re not great enough to get someone else interested in co-founding, or they’re in a city where nobody is doing what they want to do, or they just want to work with their friends and they don’t care.

2. If your co-founder is someone you don’t know well, you need to be careful not to be fooled. You may think someone is great at a job they have now, but they might not be great at what you need to do. If you have a friend you’ve known for years, you have a lot of good evidence of their intelligence and judgment.

3. It is much easier to trust someone you know well. Suppose I make a mistake in a restaurant, and I apologize to you for it. Here are two possible apologies:

A: “I’m sorry I said that. It was really rude, and I was thinking of something else at the time. It was a mistake.”

B: “I’m sorry I said that. It was really rude, and there are a bunch of reasons why I did it that are too complicated to explain, but it wasn’t a mistake.”

The first apology seems pretty good. The second one seems pretty bad.

But what if I had said:

C: “I’m sorry I said that. It was really rude, and I was thinking of something else at the time. That wasn’t a mistake.”

Or:

D: “I’m sorry I said that. It was really rude, and there are a bunch of reasons why I did it that are too complicated to explain. That wasn’t a mistake.”

I think the first two are better than the second two. This is a weird thing to think, because I’m talking about the person who said “I’m sorry, but it wasn’t a mistake”, and I think that’s worse than the person who said “I’m sorry, and it was a mistake”.

The point of the apology isn’t to get away with not having to admit you did something wrong. The point of the apology is to let the person you hurt know that you realize they were hurt and you care about it.

If you say “I’m sorry I said that. It was really rude, and there are a bunch of reasons why I did it that are too complicated to explain”, I think you’re just being defensive.

You’re not admitting you did something wrong. You’re just saying “I can see how that might hurt you, but here’s why it’s not my fault”. It’s a cop-out.

prompt: I'm 34 and I've realized I don't really know how to make friends as an adult without a structure like school or a job forcing it. write an essay about why adult friendship is so hard to start, ideally something that doesn't end with 'just join a club'
response:
A few years ago I was sitting with a few friends at a restaurant when a friend of a friend came in to join us. He was a little late, so when he got to the table he said “Sorry I’m late, my friend’s apartment was on fire.” Everyone at the table started laughing, except me. I asked “What happened?” and he said “I don’t know, it just happened.”

I didn’t understand. It was hard for me to wrap my head around something like that happening. I thought of it as a kind of surrealism.

I’ve since learned that that’s kind of normal. That’s just something that happens, sometimes.

But what I think is really interesting is that it’s a kind of surrealism that people have come to expect. In some ways, I think that’s one of the hallmarks of adulthood. Things can be surreal, but you have to just accept it. That’s just how things are.

I think that’s a big reason why adult friendships are hard to start.

I’ve seen a lot of advice that says “Just do stuff in real life! Find a club! Join a community!” I think that’s good advice, but it’s not enough. It’s not even the hard part.

I think the hardest part is to understand that things will be surreal. You will have to learn to accept that.

If you’re looking for a new friend, you’re going to meet someone that’s kind of weird. Maybe they’re really eccentric. Maybe they have a different sense of humor. Maybe they don’t have a lot of experience in the same things you do.

That’s okay. That’s just how it is.

It’s hard to accept that because it’s not the way we learn to make friends in school. In school, we’re surrounded by people who are similar to us. We’re all in the same grade. We’re all around the same age. We’re all in the same school.

When we’re in college, it’s a little bit different. We’re still surrounded by people who are similar to us, but there’s a little more diversity.

But when we’re in the real world, it’s a whole different story. We’re surrounded by people who are all over the place. Some of them are really young. Some of them are really old. Some of them are really experienced. Some of them are really inexperienced. Some of them are really weird. Some of them are really normal.

It’s hard to accept that because we’re not used to it. We’re used to being surrounded by people who are similar to us. We’re used to being in a group where everyone is on the same page.

But that’s not how the real world works. The real world is a lot more diverse than that. And that’s okay. That’s just how it is.

If you’re looking for a new friend, you’re going to meet someone that’s kind of weird. Maybe they’re really eccentric. Maybe they have a different sense of humor. Maybe they don’t have a lot of experience in the same things you do.

That’s okay. That’s just how it is.

prompt: Is nostalgia actually about the past, or is it about the person we were then? Something essayistic, not a psych textbook summary.
response:
Nostalgia is not really about the past.

It’s about who we were in the past.

When people talk about the past, they’re not really talking about the past. They’re talking about the person they were in the past.

When you hear people say “I miss the 90s,” what they really mean is “I miss who I was in the 90s.”

The 90s were just as bad back then as they are now. It was just that the person you were back then was happy.

So when you feel nostalgic, what you’re really missing is the person you were back then.

And that person is gone. Forever.

And that is what makes it so painful.

prompt: the case for ugly fonts
response:
I am not a typography person. I have a vague sense that fonts with serifs are more formal and fonts without are more casual, but that's about it.

So the other day, when I was looking at my bank's online account, I was surprised to notice that the numbers in the account balances are rendered in a very strange font. The font is "ugly". It looks like a 1970s version of Comic Sans. It's the least attractive thing on the page, and I'm surprised the bank hasn't fixed it.

But then I realized what it's for. It's a way to distinguish digits from letters. This font makes it so that you can never be confused about whether a character is a digit or a letter, because the digits look completely different from the letters.

The font is ugly, but it's a pretty good idea, and I've realized that I don't see this font trick anywhere else. So now I'm going to try to think of more places where it would be good.

The first place is probably in code. If you have a programming language that uses a digit as a valid character in a name, you can accidentally have a variable called "o" that you think is the digit "0". A lot of people like to use a font that makes these look different, but that font trick is a lot less effective than just using a font that makes all the digits look weird. It's not so easy to do that with a font, but some programming languages could just use that ugly font for all digits.

This is probably a very bad idea, because it would make everything look weird. But maybe a good compromise would be to use the ugly font for the digits that are most confusing with letters, like "1", "0", and "3".

I also realized that this is a really good idea for writing checks. People try to cheat the banks by writing checks that are ambiguous between digits and letters, but if you make the digits look weird, then the bank can see that it's a digit instead of a letter.

prompt: I'd like an essay arguing that museum wall text has become too long and too interpretive, and that it gets between the viewer and the work. Please engage seriously with the counterargument that it makes art more accessible.
response:
I don’t know if you’ve ever noticed, but the wall text accompanying paintings in museums has gotten a lot longer over the last few years.

I noticed this during my last trip to the Metropolitan Museum of Art, where I spent a couple of hours looking at the old masters. It was a beautiful, peaceful experience. And yet the wall text was so long and so interpretive that it seemed to be in the way.

In the past, the wall text would just be a simple statement of fact:

Renaissance, ca. 1500, oil on canvas, 89 x 120 cm.

That’s it. If you wanted to know more, you could always ask an attendant, or buy the book that goes with the exhibition.

Nowadays, though, the wall text looks more like this:

The artist uses a dark, brooding palette to explore the psychological complexities of his subjects. The composition draws the eye to the central figure, whose expression conveys a sense of inner turmoil. The brushwork is loose and expressive, suggesting the influence of the Romantic movement.

It’s not wrong, exactly, but it’s a lot of words. It’s a lot of interpretive, subjective stuff.

And it’s so much text that I found myself reading it instead of looking at the paintings.

I like the idea of museums being a place to go where you can just look at things. I like the idea that you can look at a painting and just enjoy it, without having to read a bunch of text about it.

But now the wall text is so long that it’s in the way. I have to read it. It’s like the text is saying, “I’m here, I’m here, look at me, not the painting.”

And it’s not just the length of the text that’s the problem. It’s also the tone of the text. It’s so interpretive. It’s like the text is telling you how to feel about the painting. And that’s not a good thing.

I know that museums are trying to make art more accessible. I get that. But I think they’re going about it the wrong way.

I think the best way to make art more accessible is to let people just look at it. To let them have their own experience with it. To let them make their own interpretations.

But the wall text is in the way. It’s too long. It’s too interpretive. And it’s getting in the way of people having their own experience with the art.

So I think it’s time for museums to start cutting back on the wall text. Let people just look at the art. Let them have their own experience with it. And if they want to know more, they can always ask an attendant, or buy the book that goes with the exhibition.

prompt: Session drummer here, 20+ years. Write an essay on why perfectly quantized drums make records feel dead, and what 'feel' actually is in measurable terms — microtiming, the push and pull around the beat. Readers will be musicians, so don't dumb it down.
response:
A few years ago I was sitting with a producer who was trying to get a drum sound he liked. He’d got the drum sound, the mic placement, the room, the amp, all that. What he wanted was to “make it feel more like the drums on this record.”

I asked him what he meant by that. He said, “You know, just a little more feel.”

I said, “I think I know what you’re talking about.”

He said, “Yeah, you do. It’s just a little bit of something.”

I said, “Yeah, we’ve got it.”

He said, “I don’t know what it is, but I know what I mean.”

I said, “Okay, well, let’s see if we can’t find it.”

And we went through the whole session, and I kept saying, “That sounds like it’s got more feel,” and he kept saying, “Yeah, it does.”

And then we got to the end of the session, and I said, “Okay, now let’s listen to the original, and then we’ll listen to the one we just did.”

And he said, “Okay.”

And we listened to the original, and then we listened to the one we just did, and he said, “Yeah, that sounds like it’s got more feel.”

I said, “Yeah, I know.”

He said, “I don’t know what you did, but it sounds better.”

I said, “Okay, well, I’m going to go home and figure out what I did.”

And I did. And I’m going to tell you what it was.

It was that I had played the drums a little bit behind the beat.

Not a lot. Just a little bit. Maybe 20 milliseconds.

But that 20 milliseconds made all the difference in the world.

It made the drums feel like they were pushing against the beat, and that’s what makes music feel alive.

It’s what makes music feel like it’s got a pulse.

It’s what makes music feel like it’s got a heartbeat.

And that’s what “feel” is.

It’s not something you can measure with a metronome.

It’s not something you can program into a drum machine.

It’s something that you have to feel in your body.

It’s something that you have to play with your heart.

And that’s why you can’t buy it.

You can’t download it.

You can’t quantize it.

You can’t grid it.

You can’t time-stretch it.

You can’t pitch-shift it.

You can’t sample it.

You can’t loop it.

You can’t layer it.

You can’t edit it.

You can’t mix it.

You can’t master it.

You can’t produce it.

You can’t record it.

You can’t play it.

You can only feel it.

And if you can’t feel it, then you don’t have it.

And if you don’t have it, then you don’t have music.

You have noise.

You have data.

You have information.

You have a file.

You have a waveform.

You have a sample.

You have a loop.

prompt: Why do we find unfinished things (sketches, demos, abandoned buildings) more moving than finished ones sometimes? Explore it.
response:
This is a common experience. Why are unfinished buildings more beautiful than completed buildings? Why is a rough draft often more beautiful than the final version? Why are sketches often more beautiful than the finished painting?

The answer lies in the human capacity for pattern completion. Our brain is a prediction machine. It’s always trying to predict what will happen next. When we see an unfinished thing, we unconsciously try to imagine the completion. This creates a certain kind of beauty in the observer. And it’s an individual beauty. Because different people will imagine different completions, and each completion will be unique to the person.

This is why a sketch can be more beautiful than a finished painting. The sketch leaves so much room for our imagination to complete the image. When we look at a finished painting, there’s nothing left for our imagination to do. We can only imagine what the person who created it was thinking. But when we look at a sketch, our imagination can take over. We can imagine the whole picture. We can imagine what it was going to be. We can imagine the story behind it. We can imagine the person who created it.

A finished painting is a dead object. A sketch is a living object. It’s a living object because it has the potential to become something else. It has the potential to become a finished painting. It has the potential to become a story. It has the potential to become a whole world.

And that’s what makes it beautiful. It’s not the thing itself that’s beautiful. It’s the potential that’s beautiful.
